title: The Pivot: Where Did Submit Go?
description: Trace a form submit from URL to controller to view to $this->input->post(), and see exactly where GET and POST send your data.
congratsText: You mastered the pivot — you can trace a submit end to end through CI3!
objectives: Explain how a CI3 controller catches an incoming request
Load a view from a controller method without opening it directly
Match a URL's segments to the correct controller and method
Identify how GET exposes submitted data in the address bar
Apply controller/method matching rules to the default index() method
Contrast POST's request-body delivery with GET's URL delivery
Read CI3's 404 page to identify what failed to match
Use $this->input->method() to confirm which HTTP method sent a request
Explain why the name attribute controls what post() can read
Trace a full submit end to end and pinpoint which link broke
recap: A CI3 controller is a PHP class that catches a request before anything else runs
Views hold only HTML and are shown only when a controller method loads them
A URL reads as controller/method, and mismatches produce a 404 instead of a guess
GET puts every field's value into the visible query string after the ?
The default index() method still follows the same controller/method matching rules
POST sends the same fields through the request body, invisible in the URL
CI3's 404 page is real HTML that usually names the exact thing it couldn't find
$this->input->method() reports whether the current request was sent as GET or POST
$this->input->post() returns an array of submitted fields keyed by their name attributes
A missing or duplicated name attribute is a common reason post() data goes missing
Tracing a submit end to end — URL, controller, view, and post() — pinpoints exactly which link broke

chunks.text: A CI3 controller is a PHP class that catches a web request before anything else runs.

check.question: Is a controller the first thing that catches an incoming URL request?

chunks.text: Each method inside a controller matches one job — visiting a URL runs exactly one matching method.

check.question: Does one controller method run for a single visited URL?

chunks.text: The file name and class name must match and both start with a capital letter, like Pivot.php holding class Pivot.

check.question: Should the file stay named pivot.php (lowercase) if the class is Pivot?

quiz.question: Which class declaration correctly matches a file named Pivot.php in CI3?

chunks.text: A view is a separate file that holds only the HTML shown to the user — never business logic.

check.question: Does a view file usually hold only HTML/display markup?

chunks.text: A controller method loads a view with $this->load->view('view_name'), leaving off the .php ending.

check.question: Do you include .php when calling load->view()?

chunks.text: A view file is never opened by double-clicking it — a controller method has to load it first.

check.question: Can a student double-click login_view.php and see it work correctly on its own?
options: No, a controller must load it

quiz.question: Arrange the steps in the order they happen when a student visits the login form's URL.

chunks.text: A CI3 URL reads as controller / method — the first segment picks the class, the second picks the function inside it.

check.question: In /pivot/hello, does 'pivot' name the controller?

chunks.text: If the method name in the URL doesn't exist in the controller, CI3 shows a 404 page instead of guessing.

check.question: Does CI3 guess the closest matching method name if you misspell it?

chunks.text: The controller name in the URL is lowercase, but the class definition itself is capitalized.

check.question: Do /pivot/hello and class Pivot use different capitalization on purpose?

quiz.question: A controller file Order.php has a method named submit(). Which URL runs it?

sections.title: GET Puts Data in the URL

chunks.text: When a form uses method="get", the browser tacks every field's value onto the end of the URL after a question mark.

check.question: Does GET add form data to the address bar?

chunks.text: That means anything typed into a GET form — even a password — sits in plain sight in the address bar and browser history.

check.question: Is a password typed into a GET form safe from being seen in the URL?

chunks.text: The query string is the part of the URL after the ?, made of name=value pairs joined by &.

check.question: Does the query string start right after the ? character?

quiz.question: A GET login form submits username and password. Type the single character that starts the query string in the resulting URL.

chunks.text: If you visit a controller URL with no method segment, like /pivot, CI3 tries to run a method named index() by default.

check.question: Does CI3 look for a method called index() when no method is given in the URL?

chunks.text: This default only saves typing — the index() method still needs to exist in the controller like any other method.

check.question: Does index() still need to be written into the controller like any other method?

chunks.text: Everything you learned about matching URL segments to controller and method names still applies to index() too.

check.question: Does the same controller/method naming rule apply to index()?

quiz.question: A controller Cart.php has methods index() and checkout(). Which URL runs checkout(), not index()?

chunks.text: Switching a form to method="post" sends the same fields, but they travel in the request body instead of the URL.

check.question: With POST, does form data still travel visibly in the URL?
options: No, it stays in the request body

chunks.text: Because POST data isn't in the URL, refreshing a POST result page can trigger a 'resubmit form' warning from the browser.

check.question: Can refreshing after a POST submit sometimes ask you to resubmit?

chunks.text: Changing method="get" to method="post" is the only change needed — the form's action and fields stay the same.

check.question: Do the field names need to change when switching GET to POST?
options: Yes, all fields must be renamed

quiz.question: Arrange the steps in the order they happen when a POST login form is submitted.
tokens: Browser sends the fields in the request body
correctOrder: Browser sends the fields in the request body

chunks.text: When CI3 can't match a URL to any real controller or method, it shows its own error page instead of a blank screen.

check.question: Does CI3 show a blank white screen when nothing matches?
options: No, it shows an error page

chunks.text: That error page is real HTML built by CI3 itself, visible if you right-click and View Page Source.

check.question: Is CI3's 404 page actual HTML generated by the framework?

chunks.text: The 404 page's message usually names the exact controller or method CI3 went looking for, which helps you spot typos fast.

check.question: Does the 404 message name the specific thing CI3 couldn't find?

quiz.question: A student visits index.php/pivott/store (typo in the controller name). What does CI3 do?
options: Shows a 404 page naming the missing controller
Silently loads the pivot controller anyway, with no warning

chunks.text: CI3 gives you a shortcut to check which HTTP method sent the current request: $this->input->method().

check.question: Does $this->input->method() tell you GET or POST was used?

chunks.text: This is handy for debugging when a form's behavior doesn't match what you expected from its method attribute.

check.question: Is checking the method a useful debugging step when POST data seems missing?

chunks.text: Calling $this->input->get() on a POST-submitted form returns nothing, because GET and POST are separate buckets.

check.question: Does $this->input->get() see data sent by a POST form?

quiz.question: A form uses method="post" and a controller runs echo $this->input->method();. Type the exact word that prints.

chunks.text: $this->input->post() returns an array of every field the form sent, keyed by each input's name attribute.

check.question: Is the array from $this->input->post() keyed by the name attribute?

chunks.text: print_r() is a quick way to dump that whole array on screen so you can see every key and value at once.

check.question: Does print_r() show the array's keys and values together?

chunks.text: Passing a specific key, like $this->input->post('username'), returns just that one field's value instead of the whole array.

check.question: Does $this->input->post('username') return only the username value?

quiz.question: A form input has no name attribute. What happens to its value in $this->input->post()?
options: It's missing from the array entirely
It appears under the input's id instead
It causes a fatal PHP error

chunks.text: The name attribute is what CI3 uses to label each piece of submitted data — not the id, not the placeholder.

check.question: Does CI3 use the name attribute, not the id, to label submitted data?

chunks.text: Two inputs that accidentally share the same name will overwrite each other, so only the last one's value survives.

check.question: If two inputs share one name, do both values get saved?
options: No, only the last one survives

chunks.text: Checking every input has a unique, correct name attribute is one of the first things to verify when post() looks wrong.

check.question: Is checking name attributes a good first debugging step for missing post() data?

quiz.question: Arrange the tokens to build a text input named email.

chunks.text: Tracing a submit end to end: the URL segment picks the controller and method, the view holds the form, and post() reads what was typed.

check.question: Does the full trace start at the URL and end at reading the posted data?
options: No, it starts at the database

chunks.text: A missing route, a misspelled method, a missing view, or a missing name attribute each break a different link in that same chain.

check.question: Can different mistakes break different links in the same chain?
options: No, only one mistake is possible

chunks.text: Reading the exact wording of CI3's error message is usually the fastest way to tell which link in the chain broke.

check.question: Is reading the error message text a fast way to find which step failed?

quiz.question: A POST form submits with no CI3 error page, but print_r($this->input->post()) shows an empty array. What's the most likely cause?
options: An input field is missing its name attribute
The controller Pivot.php doesn't exist anywhere
The method name in the URL is misspelled
The view file was never created for this form
